papers.title: SAE-RNA: A Sparse Autoencoder Model for Interpreting RNA Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How and what do RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-RNA, a sparse autoencoder model that interprets RNA language model representations by discovering sparse features aligned with biological structures and ncRNA families.
papers.conclusion: SAE-RNA provides a method for concept discovery in pretrained RNA LM embeddings, enabling interpretation without retraining and offering features for downstream tasks like feature-aware fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features localize in structurally meaningful regions such as stems and hairpins.
Features exhibit sequence biases like poly-G/C/A/U tracts that map onto secondary-structure contexts.
Deeper layers transition from diffuse to type-selective activations, with a small subset of channels preferentially firing for specific ncRNA families.
The last layer shows diminished signal, suggesting late-stage representational compression.
Features can be annotated using LLM prompting to align with known biological motifs.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints restricted the scale of training data used for the SAE models.
SAE training outcomes can vary depending on hyperparameter choices, such as sparsity setting, which may influence the granularity and stability of learned features.
future_direction: Feature-aware fine-tuning with SAE-derived features for downstream RNA tasks.
papers.abstract: Deep learning, particularly with the advancement of Large Language Models, has transformed biomolecular modeling, with protein advances (e.g., ESM) inspiring emerging RNA language models such as RiNALMo. Yet how and what these RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families remains unclear. We present SAE- RNA, interpretability model that analyzes RiNALMo representations and maps them to known human-level biological features. Our work frames RNA interpretability as concept discovery in pretrained embeddings, without end-to-end retraining, and provides practical tools to probe what RNA LMs may encode about ncRNA families. The model can be extended to close comparisons between RNA groups, and supporting hypothesis generation about previously unrecognized relationships.

papers.title: Learning Causal Representations of Single Cells via Sparse Mechanism Shift Modeling
papers.research_question: How can we learn causal representations of single-cell genomics data by modeling perturbations as interventions on latent variables, leveraging the sparse mechanism shift assumption to improve disentanglement, causal target identification, and out-of-domain generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes sVAE+, a Bayesian variant of the sparse VAE for single-cell perturbation data, which models perturbations as stochastic interventions on a sparse subset of latent variables, and demonstrates that it outperforms existing methods in disentanglement, causal target identification, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: Modeling perturbations as interventions with sparse mechanism shift enables learning causal representations that are more interpretable and generalize better, offering a promising approach for single-cell genomics and perturbation biology.
papers.key_findings:
sVAE+ achieves higher disentanglement scores (MCC) compared to VAE, β-VAE, iVAE, and sVAE on simulated data.
sVAE+ better recovers the causal graph (higher precision, recall, F1) of intervention targets in latent space.
sVAE+ improves out-of-domain generalization, yielding lower interventional negative log-likelihood on held-out perturbations.
On real single-cell perturbation datasets, sVAE+ outperforms other methods in transfer learning tasks.
The sparse mechanism shift assumption is beneficial for learning interpretable causal representations from single-cell perturbation data.
papers.limitation:
The sparsity assumption may be limiting due to indirect downstream effects in biological systems, especially as time passes after the initial perturbation.
The model assumes discrete interventions and may not handle time-resolved measurements without extension.
future_direction: Incorporating time-resolved measurements from single-cell perturbation experiments.
Handling non-sparse interactions and feedback mechanisms in biological pathways.
Extending the noise model to more realistic distributions for scRNA-seq data.
papers.abstract: Latent variable models such as the Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) have become a go-to tool for analyzing biological data, especially in the field of single-cell genomics. One remaining challenge is the interpretability of latent variables as biological processes that define a cell's identity. Outside of biological applications, this problem is commonly referred to as learning disentangled representations. Although several disentanglement-promoting variants of the VAE were introduced, and applied to single-cell genomics data, this task has been shown to be infeasible from independent and identically distributed measurements, without additional structure. Instead, recent methods propose to leverage non-stationary data, as well as the sparse mechanism shift assumption in order to learn disentangled representations with a causal semantic. Here, we extend the application of these methodological advances to the analysis of single-cell genomics data with genetic or chemical perturbations. More precisely, we propose a deep generative model of single-cell gene expression data for which each perturbation is treated as a stochastic intervention targeting an unknown, but sparse, subset of latent variables. We benchmark these methods on simulated single-cell data to evaluate their performance at latent units recovery, causal target identification and out-of-domain generalization. Finally, we apply those approaches to two real-world large-scale gene perturbation data sets and find that models that exploit the sparse mechanism shift hypothesis surpass contemporary methods on a transfer learning task. We implement our new model and benchmarks using the scvi-tools library, and release it as open-source software at https://github.com/Genentech/sVAE.

papers.title: Interpretable LLM Guardrails via Sparse Representation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior to mitigate harmful, misleading, or biased content using sparse representation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SRS, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to disentangle activations into monosemantic features and steer LLM behavior via sparse steering vectors, achieving fine-grained control while preserving output quality.
papers.conclusion: SRS enables precise and interpretable steering of LLM behavior using sparse representations, providing a reliable guardrail for safety, fairness, and truthfulness with superior performance over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRS outperforms existing steering methods like CAA and SAE-TS in single-attribute and multi-attribute control tasks.
SRS maintains high linguistic quality, including grammatical correctness and language diversity, with minimal side effects.
SRS demonstrates robustness against diverse jailbreak prompts, achieving high defense rates.
Multi-attribute control with PCA composition strategy yields the best trade-off between control effectiveness and content quality.
Sparse features enable interpretable identification of attribute-relevant dimensions through KL divergence analysis.
papers.limitation: Multi-attribute steering strategies such as PCA may not fully capture complex relationships and conflicts between attributes.
future_direction: Layer-wise or component-wise multi-attribute steering to align interventions with semantic levels.
Context-aware and personalized steering based on semantic subdomains of prompts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities in generation tasks but are prone to producing harmful, misleading, or biased content, posing significant ethical and safety concerns. To mitigate such risks, representation engineering, which steer model behavior toward desired attributes by injecting carefully designed steering vectors into LLM's representations at inference time, has emerged as a promising alternative to fine-tuning approaches. However, due to the semantically entangled nature of LLM's representation, existing representation engineering methods still suffer from several limitations: limited fine-grained controllability, content quality degradation, and conflict in multi-attribute control. To overcome these challenges, we propose Sparse Representation Steering (SRS), a novel framework that achieves fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior by first disentangling internal activations into a sparse, semantically meaningful representation space, and then selectively steering relevant dimensions. Specifically, SRS leverages a pretrained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to transform dense, entangled activation patterns into a sparse monosemantic feature space. To identify relevant features, SRS contrasts sparse activations from positive and negative prompt pairs and measures their bidirectional KL divergence to locate dimensions most associated with the target attribute. We conduct comprehensive experiments on Gemma-2 series model across three alignment dimensions, i.e., safety, fairness, and truthfulness, to evaluate the effectiveness of SRS. Results show that SRS consistently outperforms existing steering methods, which achieves significantly improved controllability across both single and multiple attribute settings, while preserving high linguistic quality and general ability.

papers.title: Maximum entropy methods for extracting the learned features of deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural networks and extract the features they learn from input data using maximum entropy methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a maximum entropy method for interpreting deep neural networks by sampling sequences that preserve penultimate layer activations, allowing extraction of learned features such as motifs and nucleosome positioning signals.
papers.conclusion: The maximum entropy method provides a valuable tool for interpreting deep neural networks, particularly in biological sequence analysis, and demonstrates synergy between statistical physics and machine learning for extracting subtle sequence features.
papers.key_findings:
The MaxEnt method successfully captures XOR logic learned by a simple ANN, while Saliency Map and DeepLIFT methods fail to do so.
The MaxEnt method localizes CTCF binding motifs with better agreement with conventional motif discovery tools (MEME/FIMO) than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The MaxEnt method extracts nucleosome positioning signals, including periodic GC content at 10 bp intervals, more effectively than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The method can assess the importance of global sequence features (e.g., GC content) via a feature importance score derived from the variance of MCMC samples.
Features extracted by MaxEnt (low-variance principal components) can be used for classification, as demonstrated by a nearest neighbor classifier achieving 76% accuracy.
papers.limitation: The MaxEnt method is computationally expensive compared to Saliency Map and DeepLIFT due to MCMC sampling.
papers.abstract: New architectures of multilayer artificial neural networks and new methods for training them are rapidly revolutionizing the application of machine learning in diverse fields, including business, social science, physical sciences, and biology. Interpreting deep neural networks, however, currently remains elusive, and a critical challenge lies in understanding which meaningful features a network is actually learning. We present a general method for interpreting deep neural networks and extracting network-learned features from input data. We describe our algorithm in the context of biological sequence analysis. Our approach, based on ideas from statistical physics, samples from the maximum entropy distribution over possible sequences, anchored at an input sequence and subject to constraints implied by the empirical function learned by a network. Using our framework, we demonstrate that local transcription factor binding motifs can be identified from a network trained on ChIP-seq data and that nucleosome positioning signals are indeed learned by a network trained on chemical cleavage nucleosome maps. Imposing a further constraint on the maximum entropy distribution also allows us to probe whether a network is learning global sequence features, such as the high GC content in nucleosome-rich regions. This work thus provides valuable mathematical tools for interpreting and extracting learned features from feed-forward neural networks.

papers.title: The cell as a token: high-dimensional geometry in language models and cell embeddings
papers.research_question: How can advances in understanding the geometry of language model embeddings inform the analysis of single-cell genomics data?
papers.core_contribution: This review highlights how principles from language model embeddings, such as context-dependence and low-dimensional manifolds, can guide the development and interpretation of single-cell foundation models.
papers.conclusion: Drawing parallels between language models and single-cell embeddings reveals shared principles in high-dimensional geometry, but biological context is more complex, requiring future models to integrate multimodal data and address dynamical processes.
papers.key_findings:
The distributional hypothesis in language, which links word meaning to context, can be analogously applied to single-cell data for self-supervised learning of cell embeddings.
Low-dimensional manifolds in embedding spaces capture semantic relationships in language and developmental pathways in biology, enabling analogies and trajectory inference.
Dynamic embeddings that incorporate context, such as through self-attention in language models or spatial data in cells, improve representation fidelity and disambiguation.
Interpretability methods like linear probes and sparse autoencoders, used in language models, can be adapted to analyze internal representations in single-cell foundation models for feature identification.
The analogy between cells and tokens has limitations due to the ordered, discrete nature of language context versus the multiscale, indirect context of biological systems.
papers.limitation: Biological context is multiscale, incomplete, and indirect compared to the discrete, ordered sequences in language, limiting direct analogies.
future_direction: Integrating diverse experimental contexts and multimodal data without loss of biological specificity in cell embeddings.
Developing improved benchmarks to test the ability of foundation models to parse complex and indirect regulatory logic in biology.
Creating temporally aware embedding models that capture continuous trajectories and causal relationships in dynamical biological systems.
papers.abstract: Single-cell sequencing technology maps cells to a high-dimensional space encoding their internal activity. Recently-proposed virtual cell models extend this concept, enriching cells' representations based on patterns learned from pretraining on vast cell atlases. This review explores how advances in understanding the structure of natural language embeddings informs ongoing efforts to analyze single-cell datasets. Both fields process unstructured data by partitioning datasets into tokens embedded within a high-dimensional vector space. We discuss how the context of tokens influences the geometry of embedding space, and how low-dimensional manifolds shape this space's robustness and interpretation. We highlight how new developments in foundation models for language, such as interpretability probes and in-context reasoning, can inform efforts to construct cell atlases and train virtual cell models.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: Towards Inference-time Category-wise Safety Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we steer LLM generations to safety using gradient-free, inference-time steering methods? The paper explores category-specific steering vectors and sophisticated extraction methods for safety steering.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a category-specific inference-time safety steering method for LLMs that uses steering vectors computed from harmful and harmless activations, with unsupervised and guided extraction methods and pruning to improve steering performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates effective category-specific inference-time safety steering for LLMs using activation-based steering vectors, providing best practices and highlighting trade-offs between safety and text quality.
papers.key_findings:
Category-specific steering reduces unsafe responses, with varying effectiveness across harm categories and models.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves safety steering and can retain or improve text quality.
Using generic harmless data (e.g., Alpaca Instructions) for steering vectors can be effective, reducing the need for category-specific harmless data.
Guided activations (filtered by an external safety classifier) can further reduce unsafe responses but may degrade text quality.
The method works better for Llama3-8B than Llama2-7B, and there is a trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.limitation:
Only attention activations were used for steering; other activation types (MLP, residual stream, block outputs) were not explored.
A simple pruning method based on L2 norms was used; more sophisticated pruning could be explored.
The method does not optimize for text quality, leading to potential degradation in helpfulness and coherence.
future_direction: Explore other types of activations or combinations for steering.
Develop better pruning methods to obtain cleaner steering signals.
Add constraints to the steered generation to improve the trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have seen unprecedented advancements in capabilities and applications across a variety of use-cases, safety alignment of these models is still an area of active research. The fragile nature of LLMs, even models that have undergone extensive alignment and safety training regimes, warrants additional safety steering steps via training-free, inference-time methods. While recent work in the area of mechanistic interpretability has investigated how activations in latent representation spaces may encode concepts, and thereafter performed representation engineering to induce such concepts in LLM outputs, the applicability of such for safety is relatively under-explored. Unlike recent inference-time safety steering works, in this paper we explore safety steering of LLM outputs using: (i) category-specific steering vectors, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the steering, and (ii) sophisticated methods for extracting informative steering vectors for more effective safety steering while retaining quality of the generated text. We demonstrate our exploration on multiple LLMs and datasets, and showcase the effectiveness of the proposed steering method, along with a discussion on the implications and best practices.

papers.title: Transformers and the representation of biomedical background knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether transformer-based models encode biomedical domain knowledge at entity and relational levels, how they handle complex facts, differences between models, and their response to evidence biases in the literature.
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformer-based models encode biomedical knowledge, but fine-tuning can lose some semantic structure, and it highlights risks of misclassification due to dataset biases.
papers.conclusion: Transformers encode biomedical knowledge useful for inference, but careful evaluation is needed due to biases and information loss during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers like BioBERT and BioMegatron encode biomedical domain knowledge at entity and relational levels.
Fine-tuning for specific tasks can lead to loss of semantic information about entity types.
Clustering analysis shows that representations form biologically meaningful groups, such as genes from the same pathways.
Classification errors are correlated with the frequency of entities in the training data, indicating bias.
Despite strong evidence, some well-known clinical relations can be misclassified by the models.
papers.limitation: Models may misclassify well-known clinical relations due to biases in the dataset.
papers.abstract: Specialised transformers-based models (such as BioBERT and BioMegatron) are adapted for the biomedical domain based on publicly available biomedical corpora. As such, they have the potential to encode large-scale biological knowledge. We investigate the encoding and representation of biological knowledge in these models, and its potential utility to support inference in cancer precision medicine - namely, the interpretation of the clinical significance of genomic alterations. We compare the performance of different transformer baselines; we use probing to determine the consistency of encodings for distinct entities; and we use clustering methods to compare and contrast the internal properties of the embeddings for genes, variants, drugs and diseases. We show that these models do indeed encode biological knowledge, although some of this is lost in fine-tuning for specific tasks. Finally, we analyse how the models behave with regard to biases and imbalances in the dataset.

papers.title: Steering Language Models in Multi-Token Generation: A Case Study on Tense and Aspect
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the grammatical features of tense and aspect internally, and how can we causally control these features during multi-token generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies orthogonal directions for tense and aspect in LLM residual space using LDA and demonstrates causal control via steering, showing that effective steering depends on strength, location, and duration to minimize side effects like topic shift and degeneration.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLMs encode tense and aspect in orthogonal, human-like grammatical structures, and steering can verify causality but requires careful tuning of parameters to avoid side effects, indicating it is not yet a perfect control method.
papers.key_findings:
Tense and aspect are encoded as distinct, orthogonal directions in residual space, forming structured subspaces.
Steering these directions can causally control the grammatical features in multi-token generation across different tasks.
Steering effectiveness varies by task and target, with tense easier to steer than aspect, and is influenced by activation norms and model architecture.
Steering strength, location, and duration are crucial parameters; improper settings lead to side effects like topic shift and degeneration.
Subtracting the source concept vector (TA+SS) can reduce selectivity, but projection subtraction (TA+Proj-SS) mitigates this issue.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on English, which has a very regular inflection system, and tense and aspect are only two of six known strategies for expressing temporal information in language.
The analysis focuses on steering grammatical properties in three tasks, and side effects such as topic shift may manifest differently when steering other concepts like sentiment.
future_direction: Investigate mechanism-independent time representations (e.g., consistent representation of 'past' in different surface forms).
Explore language-independent tense representations (e.g., cross-lingual past-present contrast).
Expand the range of tasks and steering targets to identify more general conditions for effective steering.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are able to generate grammatically well-formed text, but how do they encode their syntactic knowledge internally? While prior work has focused largely on binary grammatical contrasts, in this work, we study the representation and control of two multidimensional hierarchical grammar phenomena - verb tense and aspect - and for each, identify distinct, orthogonal directions in residual space using linear discriminant analysis. Next, we demonstrate causal control over both grammatical features through concept steering across three generation tasks. Then, we use these identified features in a case study to investigate factors influencing effective steering in multi-token generation. We find that steering strength, location, and duration are crucial parameters for reducing undesirable side effects such as topic shift and degeneration. Our findings suggest that models encode tense and aspect in structurally organized, human-like ways, but effective control of such features during generation is sensitive to multiple factors and requires manual tuning or automated optimization.

papers.title: Automated Neuron Labelling Enables Generative Steering and Interpretability in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we automatically label neurons in protein language models with natural language descriptions, and how can these labels be used to steer protein generation towards desired properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automated neuron labeling framework for protein language models and a neuron activation-guided steering method to generate proteins with desired biochemical and structural properties.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework for automated neuron labeling and generative steering in protein language models, enabling interpretability and control over protein generation, and suggests future directions for integration with structural validation and model pruning.
papers.key_findings:
Automated neuron labeling produces interpretable descriptions that capture diverse biochemical and structural properties of proteins.
Neuron activation-guided steering can generate proteins with targeted characteristics, such as specific molecular weight, GRAVY score, and secondary/tertiary structural motifs.
Larger PLMs capture more fine-grained protein features and show a more distributed representation of features across layers compared to smaller models.
Feature encoding follows a hierarchical pattern: sequence-derived properties peak in early layers, structural properties in middle layers, and functional properties in later layers.
Negative steering (multiplying neuron activations by negative values) can invert the effect for some features (e.g., GRAVY score) but not for others (e.g., instability index).
papers.limitation:
LLM explainer may generate oversimplified or hallucinated descriptions.
Generated proteins may not fold into viable, stable structures due to high ΔG values.
Limited to three models due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Incorporate a reinforcement learning module with structure prediction models (e.g., AlphaFold2) to improve structural viability of generated proteins.
Extend neuron labeling to more models and use multiple LLMs for more robust labels.
Explore pruning neurons based on labels to compress models while retaining performance.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) encode rich biological information, yet their internal neuron representations are poorly understood. We introduce the first automated framework for labeling every neuron in a PLM with biologically grounded natural language descriptions. Unlike prior approaches relying on sparse autoencoders or manual annotation, our method scales to hundreds of thousands of neurons, revealing individual neurons are selectively sensitive to diverse biochemical and structural properties. We then develop a novel neuron activation-guided steering method to generate proteins with desired traits, enabling convergence to target biochemical properties like molecular weight and instability index as well as secondary and tertiary structural motifs, including alpha helices and canonical Zinc Fingers. We finally show that analysis of labeled neurons in different model sizes reveals PLM scaling laws and a structured neuron space distribution.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Identifiable Interpretation and Control in Generative Models via Causal Minimality
papers.research_question: Under what theoretical conditions can we reliably identify meaningful, interpretable latent concepts within modern generative models? And what actionable, theoretically-grounded insights can advance both interpretability and controllability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework based on causal minimality that provides conditions under which latent representations in generative models can be identified component-wise, enabling interpretable hierarchical concept graphs and fine-grained control.
papers.conclusion: The experiments illustrate the implications of the theorems and show how a principled, causal understanding can guide the application of established interpretation techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The principle of causal minimality, instantiated as sparsity constraints, enables the extraction of interpretable hierarchical concept graphs from text-to-image diffusion models.
The learned representations under these conditions are component-wise identifiable, meaning they correspond to true latent variables of the data-generating process.
These causally grounded concepts allow for fine-grained model steering, demonstrated in tasks like model unlearning, controllable generation, and multi-level editing.
papers.limitation: The theoretical assumptions, such as causal minimality and smoothness, may not hold universally in practice.
papers.abstract: Deep generative models, while revolutionizing fields like image and text generation, largely operate as opaque black boxes, hindering human understanding, control, and alignment. While methods like sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show remarkable empirical success, they often lack theoretical guarantees, risking subjective insights. Our primary objective is to establish a principled foundation for interpretable generative models. We demonstrate that the principle of causal minimality -- favoring the simplest causal explanation -- can endow the latent representations of diffusion vision and autoregressive language models with clear causal interpretation and robust, component-wise identifiable control. We introduce a novel theoretical framework for hierarchical selection models, where higher-level concepts emerge from the constrained composition of lower-level variables, better capturing the complex dependencies in data generation. Under theoretically derived minimality conditions (manifesting as sparsity or compression constraints), we show that learned representations can be equivalent to the true latent variables of the data-generating process. Empirically, applying these constraints to leading generative models allows us to extract their innate hierarchical concept graphs, offering fresh insights into their internal knowledge organization. Furthermore, these causally grounded concepts serve as levers for fine-grained model steering, paving the way for transparent, reliable systems.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Attention over learned object embeddings enables complex visual\n reasoning
papers.research_question: Can a neural-network-based approach combining learned object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning achieve state-of-the-art performance on complex visual reasoning tasks without task-specific modular components?
papers.core_contribution: The Aloe model, which combines learned object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning, achieves state-of-the-art performance on three visual reasoning tasks without task-specific modular components, demonstrating that flexibility and performance need not be traded off.
papers.conclusion: The success of Aloe suggests that with the right soft biases and learning objectives—object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning—neural networks can achieve strong performance on spatiotemporal reasoning tasks without resorting to task-specific modular components.
papers.key_findings:
Aloe outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on CLEVRER, CATER, and ACRE across various question and reasoning types.
The combination of object-level discretization, global self-attention, and self-supervised learning is crucial for strong performance; ablations of any component lead to significant drops.
Aloe is data-efficient, matching previous SOTA performance on CLEVRER with only 50-60% of the training data.
The model generalizes across three distinct visual reasoning tasks (CLEVRER, CATER, ACRE) without any architectural modifications.
Qualitative analysis of attention weights shows the model aligns objects across time and focuses on relevant objects and words for answering questions.
papers.limitation:
Applied only to synthetic datasets due to a lack of real-world datasets testing higher-order spatiotemporal reasoning.
The domains used may not fully evaluate the intended capacities due to hidden biases or other factors.
May perpetuate biases found in training data and could invite problematic applications involving automated assignment of blame.
future_direction: Applying the approach to real-world datasets, such as the upcoming Traffic QA.
Investigating other self-supervised losses and masking schemes to further improve dynamics learning.
Designing and developing more challenging tasks that better approximate human-level visual, spatiotemporal, and causal reasoning.
papers.abstract:
Neural networks have achieved success in a wide array of perceptual tasks but
often fail at tasks involving both perception and higher-level reasoning. On
these more challenging tasks, bespoke approaches (such as modular symbolic
components, independent dynamics models or semantic parsers) targeted towards
that specific type of task have typically performed better. The downside to
these targeted approaches, however, is that they can be more brittle than
general-purpose neural networks, requiring significant modification or even
redesign according to the particular task at hand. Here, we propose a more
general neural-network-based approach to dynamic visual reasoning problems that
obtains state-of-the-art performance on three different domains, in each case
outperforming bespoke modular approaches tailored specifically to the task. Our
method relies on learned object-centric representations, self-attention and
self-supervised dynamics learning, and all three elements together are required
for strong performance to emerge. The success of this combination suggests that
there may be no need to trade off flexibility for performance on problems
involving spatio-temporal or causal-style reasoning. With the right soft biases
and learning objectives in a neural network we may be able to attain the best
of both worlds.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied to dense text embeddings to extract interpretable features and enable fine-grained control over semantic search?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can effectively disentangle semantic concepts in dense text embeddings, enabling interpretable features that can be used to precisely steer semantic search.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable features from dense text embeddings, enabling enhanced control and understanding in semantic search applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn interpretable features from dense embeddings with high Pearson correlation in automated labeling.
Feature families can be identified through graph-based clustering, representing related concepts at different abstraction levels.
SAE features can be used to intervene on embeddings for fine-grained control in semantic search.
Scaling laws show power-law relationships between SAE performance and model parameters like number of latents and compute.
Features exhibit splitting and recurrence across different SAE capacities, with some universal features appearing across models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in extracting interpretable features from complex neural networks. We present one of the first applications of SAEs to dense text embeddings from large language models, demonstrating their effectiveness in disentangling semantic concepts. By training SAEs on embeddings of over 420,000 scientific paper abstracts from computer science and astronomy, we show that the resulting sparse representations maintain semantic fidelity while offering interpretability. We analyse these learned features, exploring their behaviour across different model capacities and introducing a novel method for identifying ``feature families'' that represent related concepts at varying levels of abstraction. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we show how these interpretable features can be used to precisely steer semantic search, allowing for fine-grained control over query semantics. This work bridges the gap between the semantic richness of dense embeddings and the interpretability of sparse representations. We open source our embeddings, trained sparse autoencoders, and interpreted features, as well as a web app for exploring them.

papers.title: DISCO: Disentangled Communication Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is steering the query and value representation spaces within attention heads more effective for controlling LLM behavior than steering attention head outputs or other spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCO Steering, a method that injects steering vectors directly into the query and value spaces of attention heads, providing more granular control and superior performance over existing steering vector baselines.
papers.conclusion: Query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods, and DISCO provides an effective and flexible approach for controlling LLM behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Query and value spaces exhibit higher linear discriminability of concepts compared to attention head outputs.
DISCO Steering disentangles the strong Communication Steering baseline, allowing independent control of query and value steering magnitudes.
DISCO achieves the best performance in 13 out of 16 experiments across multiple datasets and models.
Steering query spaces dynamically re-weights attention, while steering value spaces directly adds to the head output.
The method is effective for promoting and suppressing behaviors like truthfulness, power-seeking, wealth-seeking, and corrigibility.
papers.limitation:
Requires a dataset of positive and negative examples for each concept.
Steering vectors are linear, which may not capture nonlinear concepts.
Could be misused for jailbreaks or generating inappropriate content.
future_direction: Extending DISCO to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder, multimodal).
Exploring nonlinear steering vectors.
Applying DISCO to more complex behaviors and real-world applications.
papers.abstract: A variety of recent methods guide large language model outputs via the inference-time addition of steering vectors to residual-stream or attention-head representations. In contrast, we propose to inject steering vectors directly into the query and value representation spaces within attention heads. We provide evidence that a greater portion of these spaces exhibit high linear discriminability of concepts --a key property motivating the use of steering vectors-- than attention head outputs. We analytically characterize the effect of our method, which we term DISentangled COmmunication (DISCO) Steering, on attention head outputs. Our analysis reveals that DISCO disentangles a strong but underutilized baseline, steering attention inputs, which implicitly modifies queries and values in a rigid manner. In contrast, DISCO's direct modulation of these components enables more granular control. We find that DISCO achieves superior performance over a number of steering vector baselines across multiple datasets on LLaMA 3.1 8B and Gemma 2 9B, with steering efficacy scoring up to 19.1% higher than the runner-up. Our results support the conclusion that the query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
